Vector Spaces
The set V is called a vector space over the field F of scalars, if for
any elements a, b, c in V and any scalars α, β in F, the following
axioms are satisfied.
1. 𝑎 + 𝑏 is in V. (closure property)
2. 𝑎 + 𝑏 = 𝑏 + 𝑎. (commutative law)
3. 𝑎 + 𝑏 + 𝑐 = 𝑎 + 𝑏 + 𝑐 . (associative law)
4. 𝑎 + 0 = 𝑎 = 0 + 𝑎. (existence of zero element in V)
5. 𝑎 + −𝑎 = 0. (existence of additive inverse)
The properties 1 to 5 are in accordance with respect to vector
addition defined over V.

Bernoulli Trials
• Each trial of an experiment that has only two possible outcomes (success or failure) is
called a “Bernoulli trial.”
• If p is the probability of success, then (1-p) is the probability of failure.
• The Bernoulli probability mass function is the density function of a discrete variable X
having 0 and 1 as the only possible values, i.e. P(X=1)=p and P(X=0)=1-p.
• A random variable X is said to be Bernoulli random variable if pmf satisfies above
equation for some p ∈ 0,1 .

Poisson Distribution
Poisson distribution occurs when there are two events
which do not occur as outcomes of a definite number
of trials of an experiment but which occur at random
points of time and space wherein our interest lies only
in the number of occurrences of the event, not in its
non-occurrences.

When an event occurs rarely, the number of occurrences of such an
event may be assumed to follow a Poisson distribution. The following
are some of the examples, which may be analysed using Poisson
distribution:
(i) the number of alpha particles emitted by a radioactive source
in a given time interval
(ii) the number of telephone calls received at a telephone exchange
in a given time interval
(iii) the number of defective articles in a packet of 100
(iv) the number of printing errors at each page of a book
(v) the number of road accidents reported in a city per day.

Normal Distribution
Characteristics of Normal Distribution:
• It is bell shaped and has single peak at the center of the distribution.
• The arithmetic mean, median and mode are equal.
• The total area under the curve is 1. Half the area under the normal curve
is to the left of this center point and the other half to the left of it.
• It is symmetrical about the mean 𝑥 = 𝜇 or 𝑧 = 0.
• The location of normal distribution is determined by the mean 𝜇, the
dispersion or spread of the distribution is determined by the standard
deviation 𝜎.
• For large values of 𝜎, the curve tends to flatten out
• and for small values of 𝜎, it has a sharp peak

Correlation:
In a bivariate distribution, if a change in one variable effects a change in the other variable,
then the variables are said to be correlated.
Types of Correlation:
❑ Positive Correlation: Both variables increase together (e.g., height and weight rise
together).
❑ Negative Correlation: One variable increases while the other decreases (e.g., As speed
increases, travel time decreases).
❑ Zero Correlation: No relationship between variables (e.g., shoe size and intelligence).

Vector Subspace
Let 𝑉 be a vector space over the field 𝐹 of scalars and 𝑊 be a non-
empty subset of 𝑉. Then 𝑊 is called the subspace of 𝑉 if 𝑊 itself is a
vector space over 𝐹 under the same operations of vector addition
and scalar multiplication in 𝑉.
Remark: To show that 𝑊 is a subspace of a vector space 𝑉, it is not
necessary to verify all the 10 properties. If it is shown that 𝑊 is closed
under the vector addition and scalar multiplication, then the
properties 2, 3, 7, 8, 9 and 10 are automatically satisfied because
these properties are valid for all elements in 𝑉 and hence are also
valid for all elements in 𝑊. Thus we need to verify only existence of
zero element and additive inverse in 𝑊.

Dimension and Basis
Let V be a vector space. If for some positive integer n, there exists a
set S of n linearly independent elements of V and if every set of n+1
or more elements in V is linearly dependent, then V is said to have
dimension n. We write dim (V)=n.
A basis for V is a linearly independent set of vectors in V which spans
the space V. The space V is finite-dimensional if it has a finite basis.
Remarks
1. The maximum number of linearly independent elements of V is
the dimension of V.
2. A vector space whose only element is zero has dimension zero.
3. Let { v ,v , . . . , v } be the linearly independent elements of vector
1 2 n
space V of dimension n. Then every other element of V can be
written as a linear combination of these elements. Also this
representation is unique.

Basic probability theory
To start with, a few simple definitions are presented.
Experiment An experiment is a procedure we perform (quite often hypothetical) that
produces some result. Often the letter 𝐸 is used to designate an experiment (e.g., the
experiment 𝐸 might consist of tossing a coin five times).
5
Outcome An outcome is a possible result of an experiment. e.g., an outcome of
experiment 𝐸 might represent the sequence of tosses heads-heads-tails-heads-tails;
5
however, the more concise HHTHT might also be used.
Event An event is a certain set of outcomes of an experiment (e.g., the event
𝐶 associated with experiment 𝐸 might be 𝐶= {all outcomes consisting of an even
5
number of heads}).
3

Sample Space The sample space is the collection or set of “all possible” distinct
outcomes of an experiment. The letter 𝑆 is used to designate the sample space, which
is the universal set of outcomes of an experiment. A sample space is called discrete if it
is a finite or a countably infinite set. It is called continuous or a continuum otherwise.
Classification of Events
Subset An event 𝐸 is said to be a subset of the event 𝐹 if, whenever 𝐸 occurs, 𝐹 also
occurs. This means that all of the sample points of 𝐸 are contained in 𝐹. Hence
considering 𝐸 and 𝐹 solely as two sets, 𝐸 is a subset of 𝐹 in the usual set-theoretic
sense: that is, 𝐸 ⊆ 𝐹.
4

Equality Events 𝐸 and 𝐹 are said to be equal if the occurrence of 𝐸 implies the
occurrence of 𝐹, and vice versa; that is, if 𝐸 ⊆ 𝐹 and 𝐹 ⊆ 𝐸, hence 𝐸 = 𝐹.
Intersection An event is called the intersection of two events 𝐸 and 𝐹 if it occurs only

text:
Graphical Solutions of LPP
• LPP involving two decision variables can be easily solved by graphical methods.
• To solve using graphical methods following steps are involved:
(a) Identify the problem, the decision variable, the objective function, and the
constraints.
(b) Plot a graph representing all the constraints of the problem and identify the
feasible region.
(c) Obtain the value of objective function at all the corner points of the feasible
region. (Corner Point Method)
(d) Obtain the point on the feasible region that optimizes the objective function-
the optimal solution.

sensitivity (or post-optimal) analysis.

• Fundamental Theorem of Duality: If either the
primal or the dual problems has a finite optimal
solution, then the other problem also has a finite
optimal solution, and the optimal values of the
objective functions in both the problems are the
same.
• If the primal or dual has unbounded solution, then
the other problem is infeasible.
• If the primal is infeasible, then the dual is
infeasible or unbounded.

Optimal Separating Hyperplanes
• The optimal separating hyperplane separates the two classes and maximizes the distance to the
closest point from either class (Vapnik, 1996). This provides a unique solution to the separating
hyperplane problem and maximizes the margin between the two classes on the training data.
Thus it leads to better classification performance on test data. This concept is central to the
Support Vector Machine (SVM) classifier.

Support Vector Machine (SVM):
➢
Support Vector Machine is the supervised machine learning algorithm, that is
used in both classification and regression of models. but it is most commonly
used for classification problems.
➢ SVM is an algorithm that finds the optimal separating hyperplane which
maximizes the margin between two classes in the feature space.
➢SVM tries to draw a decision boundary (hyperplane) that best separates the data
points of different classes with the widest possible margin — i.e., the distance
between the hyperplane and the nearest data points of each class should be
maximum.
➢These nearest points are called support vectors, and they are the
most critical elements in defining the hyperplane.

Random Variable
• A random variable X is a function that assigns a real number to each
outcome of the sample space S, i.e., X: S→R is a mapping from the
sample space S to the set of real numbers R.
• The sample space S is the domain of the random variable and the set of
all values taken on by the random variable is the range of the random
variable X.
• A random variable is usually denoted by an uppercase letter such as X
and the corresponding lowercase letter, such as x, denotes a possible
value of the random variable X.
• If only one characteristics is considered corresponding to the sample
space of a random experiment, then the random variable is called one
dimensional random variable.

• More than one characteristics may be considered corresponding to the
sample space of a random experiment, e.g., suppose that S consists of a
large group of students of a college. Let the experiment consist of
choosing a student at random. Let X denotes the weight of the student
and Y denotes the students' height. Then (X, Y) is a two dimensional
random variable. The same idea may be extended further.

unbiased coins simultaneously, so the random variable X can take
values 0, 1, 2 and 3, i.e.,

Discrete Random Variable
• A random variable which can assume some specific values is called a
discrete random variable.
• The main characteristic of a discrete random variable is that the set of
possible values in the range can all be listed and the list may be a finite
list or a countably infinite list.
Examples
• Number of heads obtained when 10 coins are tossed.
• Number of phone calls received, per day at a telephone booth,
• number of sixes obtained when a pair of dice are thrown.
• Number of spade cards when 4 cards are chosen from a well shuffled
pack of 52 playing cards.
• The number of odd numbers selected out of the set of positive
integers.

Continuous Random Variable
• A random variable X which can take any value in an interval of real
numbers is said to be a continuous random variable.
• The range of X can take infinitely many real values within one or
more intervals of real numbers.
• The set of all possible values in the range cannot be listed in case
of a continuous variable as the list is uncountably infinite.
Examples
• The duration of a phone call received.
• The time to failure of a machine.
• The temperature gained by an electric motor after one hour of
operation.
• The amount of rainfall in a day.

Two dimensional random variable
Let S be the sample space associated with the random
experiment E. Let X = X(s) and Y = Y(s) be two functions, each
assigning a real number to each outcome s∈S of the random
experiment, then (X, Y) is called the two dimensional random
variable.
If the possible values of (X, Y) are finite or countably infinite,
then (X, Y) is called a two-dimensional discrete random variable.
If (X, Y) can assume all values in a specified region R in the xy
plane, then (X, Y) is called a two- dimensional continuous
random variable.

text:
• The Simplex method is an efficient algorithm for solving linear
programming problems (LPPs) by iteratively moving from one vertex
of the feasible region to an adjacent vertex until an optimal solution is
found.
• It works by systematically checking the corner points of the feasible
region, defined by the constraints, to find the one that maximizes or
minimizes the objective function.
• It is applied to solve LPPs, especially those with more than two
variables or multiple constraints where the graphical method is not
feasible

text:
Key Concepts
•Slack variables:
Added to 'less than or equal to' constraints to convert them to equalities.
It represents unused resources.
It contributes nothing to the objective function value.
•Surplus variables:
Subtracted from 'greater than or equal to' constraints to convert them to equalities.
It represents an excess above a constraint requirement level.
It contributes nothing to the objective function value.
•Artificial variables:
Used for 'greater than or equal to' and equality constraints to find an initial basic feasible
solution.
They have no real meaning in the problem.
Given a very large penalty (M or –M) in the objective function so that they are removed
from the final solution.

text:
• Tableau: The problem's equations are organized into a matrix, or
tableau, which is used to perform calculations at each iteration.
• Pivot Selection:
oEntering Variable: The non-basic variable with the most negative
coefficient in the objective function row is chosen to enter the basis, as
it offers the greatest potential improvement.
oLeaving Variable: Determined by the minimum ratio test to ensure the
next solution remains feasible. This is found by dividing the right-
hand side of each constraint by its corresponding value in the pivot
column.
• Optimality Condition: The algorithm stops when all the coefficients
in the objective function row are non-negative for a maximization
problem (or non-positive for a minimization problem), indicating that
no further improvement can be made.

• Basic variables: These are the variables in a LPP that are set to a non-
zero value, while non-basic variables are set to zero.
• Basic solution: An initial solution where 𝑛−𝑚 variables are set to
zero (non-basic variables) and the remaining 𝑚 variables (basic
variables) are solved for, where 𝑛 is the total number of variables and
𝑚 is the number of constraints.
• Basic feasible solution (BFS): Basic solution which also satisfies the
no-negativity constraint.
o Degenerate BFS: If one or more basic variables are zero.
o Non-degenerate BFS: If all the basic variables are non-zero.
• Optimal BFS: BFS which optimizes the objective function.

Constrained Extremal Problems:
The optimization problems having continuous objective function and equality or
inequality type constraints are called constrained extremal problems. The solution of
such problems, having differentiable objective function and equality type constraints
can be obtained by a number of methods, but the most common is the Lagrange
Multipliers Method.

text: assigns patient IDs in the format PAT-YYYY-XXX, where: • YYYY is the year of registration (between 2000 and 2025), • XXX is a three-digit unique number (001 to 999). Write a Java program that: 1. Accepts a patient ID as input. 2. Validates the format with the following checks: • Must start with "PAT-". • The year part (YYYY) must be numeric and between 2000 and 2025. • The unique number (XXX) must be exactly 3 digits. • No extra characters or spaces should be present. 3. If the ID is valid, extract and display the year of registration and unique number. 4. If the ID is invalid, print a clear error message explaining which check failed.

subject: Theory of Computation
text:
Are there things we cannot do with
computers?
The halting problem We allow our computers unbounded memory and
unbounded time to operate. Given a fixed computer C, consider the
following task: decide (maybe, with the help of another computer, C0) for
each possible program p for C, whether when we start computer C on
program p, it will ever finish the computation?
• Solving integer equations Are there algorithmically unsolvable problems
about things other than computers? Yes. Consider an equation of the form
x^3 = 3y^6 −2x^4 −11. We are interested in finding out whether this
equation has any solution in integers. Is there any algorithm to solve all
such problems?
• Post Corespondence problem : Given two lists of words (a1, a2, .., an) and
(b1, b2, .., bn), find a sequence of indices so that the concatenated words
are equal. E.g. given the lists (1: a, 2: ab, 3: bba) and (1: baa, 2: aa, 3: bb),
the sequence (3, 2, 3, 1) is a solution since bba+ab+bba+a =
bb+aa+bb+baa. Is not possible to say whether any such PC solution exits or
not under all circumstances

subject: Theory of Computation
text:
According to the characteristics of automata, it is useful to run on some
given sequence of inputs in discrete time steps. An automaton gets one
input every time step that is picked up from a finite set of alphabets. At
any time, the symbols so far fed to the automaton as input string. At each
time step when the automaton reads an input string, it jumps or transitions
to another state that is decided by a transaction function that takes the
current state and input symbol as input parameters for the computation of
next state or output. The automaton reads the alphabets of input strings
one after another and transitions from state to state as per the transition
function rules, until the string is read completely by automation machine.
Once the input word has been read, the automaton is said to have stopped
and the state at which automaton has stopped named the final state.
Depending on the final state of the machine, it’s cleared that the
automaton either accepts or rejects an input string.

Chomsky Hierarchy
•Type 0-> Unrestricted Grammar
•Type 1-> Context Sensitive Grammar
•Type 2-> Context Free Grammar
•Type 3-> Regular Grammar

subject: Theory of Computation
text:
Grammar
• A grammar G = (V, T, S, P) consists of the
following quadruple:
– a set V of variables (non-terminal symbols),
∈
including a starting symbol S NT
– a set T of terminals (same as an alphabet, Σ)
– A start symbol S ∈ V
– a set P of production rules
• Example:
S → aS | A
A→ bA | λ

subject: Theory of Computation
text:
Derivation
• Strings are “derived” from a grammar
• Example of a derivation
⇒ ⇒ ⇒ ⇒ ⇒
S aS aaS aaA aabA aab
• At each step, a nonterminal is replaced by
the sentential form on the right-hand side
of a rule (a sentential form can contain
nonterminals and/or terminals)
• Automata recognize languages; grammars
generate languages

subject: Theory of Computation
text:
Regular grammar
• A grammar is said to be right-linear if all
productions are of the form A→xB or A→x,
where A and B are variables and x is a string of
terminals
• A grammar is said to be left-linear if all
productions are of the form A→Bx or A→x
• A regular grammar is either right-linear or
left-linear.

subject: Theory of Computation
text:
Linear grammar
• A grammar can be linear without being right-
or left-linear.
• A linear grammar is a grammar in which at
most one variable can occur on the right side
of any production rule, without any restriction
on the position of the variable.
• Example:
S → aS | A
A→ Ab | λ

subject: Theory of Computation

Context-free Grammars
A grammar G = (V, T, S, P) is said to be
context-free if all production rules in P have the
form
A → x
∈ ∈ ∪
where A V and x (V T)*
A language is said to be context-free iff there is
a context free grammar G such that L = L(G).

Context-free Grammars
Context-free means that there is a single
variable on the left side of each grammar rule.
You can imagine other kinds of grammatical
rules where this condition does not hold. For
example:
1Z1 → 101
In this rule, the variable Z goes to 0 only in the
context of a 1 on its left and a 1 to the right.
This is a context-sensitive rule.

The grammar G = ({S}, {a, b}, S, P), with
production rules:
S → aSa | bSb | λ
is context-free. This grammar is linear (that is,
there is at most a single variable on the
right-hand side of every rule), but is neither
right-linear nor left-linear (the variable is not
always the rightmost [leftmost] character on the
right-hand side of the rule), so it is not regular.

subject: Theory of Computation
text:
Regular vs. context-free
Are
regular languages context-free?
Yes, because context-free means that there is a single
variable on the left side of each grammar rule. All regular
languages are generated by grammars that have a single
variable on the left side of each grammar rule.
But, as we have seen, not all context-free grammars are
regular. So regular languages are a proper subset of the
class of context-free languages.

nonterminal is replaced at each step. In a
rightmost derivation, the rightmost nonterminal is
replaced at each step.
•Many derivations are neither leftmost nor
rightmost.
•If there is a single parse tree, there is also a
single leftmost derivation.

Decidable Problems
• A problem is said to be Decidable if we can always construct a
corresponding algorithm that can answer the problem correctly. We
can intuitively understand Decidable issues by considering a simple
example. Suppose we are asked to compute all the prime numbers in
the range of 1000 to 2000. To find the solution to this problem, we
can easily construct an algorithm that can enumerate all the prime
numbers in this range.

subject: Theory of Computation
text:
• Now talking about Decidability in terms of a Turing machine, a
problem is said to be a Decidable problem if there exists a
corresponding Turing machine that halts on every input with an
answer- yes or no. It is also important to know that these problems
are termed Turing Decidable since a Turing machine always halts on
every input, accepting or rejecting it.

subject: Theory of Computation
text:
Semi/partial Decidable Problems
• Semi-decidable problems are those for which a Turing machine halts
on the input accepted by it but it can either halt or loop forever on
the input which the Turing Machine rejects. Such problems are
termed as Turing Recognisable problems.

subject: Theory of Computation
text:
Example
• We will now consider some few important Decidable problems:
• Are two regular languages L and M equivalent: We can easily check
this by using Set Difference operation. L-M =Null and M-L =Null.
Hence (L-M) U (M-L) = Null, then L,M are equivalent.
• Membership of a CFL: We can always find whether a string exists in a
given CFL by using an algorithm based on dynamic programming.
• Emptiness of a CFL By checking the production rules of the CFL we
can easily state whether the language generates any strings or not.

subject: Theory of Computation
text:
Undecidable Problems
• The problems for which we can’t construct an algorithm that can
answer the problem correctly in finite time are termed as
Undecidable Problems. These problems may be partially decidable
but they will never be decidable. That is there will always be a
condition that will lead the Turing Machine into an infinite loop
without providing an answer at all.

subject: Theory of Computation
text:
• We can understand Undecidable Problems intuitively by
considering Fermat's Theorem, a popular Undecidable Problem
which states that no three positive integers a, b and c for any n>2 can
ever satisfy the equation: a^n + b^n = c^n. If we feed this problem to
a Turing machine to find such a solution which gives a contradiction
then a Turing Machine might run forever, to find the suitable values
of n, a, b and c. But we are always unsure whether a contradiction
exists or not and hence we term this problem as an Undecidable
Problem.

subject: Theory of Computation
text:
Example
• These are few important Undecidable Problems:
• Whether a CFG generates all the strings or not: As a Context Free Grammar (CFG)
generates infinite strings, we can’t ever reach up to the last string and hence it is
Undecidable.
• Whether two CFG L and M equal: Since we cannot determine all the strings of
any CFG, we can predict that two CFG are equal or not.
• Ambiguity of CFG: There exist no algorithm which can check whether for the
ambiguity of a Context Free Language (CFL). We can only check if any particular
string of the CFL generates two different parse trees then the CFL is ambiguous.
• Is it possible to convert a given ambiguous CFG into corresponding
non-ambiguous CFL: It is also an Undecidable Problem as there doesn’t exist any
algorithm for the conversion of an ambiguous CFL to non-ambiguous CFL.
• Is a language Learning which is a CFL, regular: This is an Undecidable Problem as
we can not find from the production rules of the CFL whether it is regular or not.

subject: Theory of Computation
text:
• Decidability and Complexity Theory lies at the heart of theoretical
computer science. It helps us understand what problems can be
solved by computers and how efficiently they can be solved. A
Decidable problem is one that can be solved by an algorithm in a
finite number of steps, while an Undecidable problem is one for
which no algorithm can provide a correct answer for all possible
inputs.

subject: Theory of Computation
text:
Decidable and Undecidable Languages
• Decidable Languages:
• A language is decidable if there exists a Turing Machine (TM) that halts on all
inputs and correctly decides whether a given string belongs to the language
or not.
• Example:
The language L={anbn∣n≥0}L = \{ a^n b^n | n \geq 0 \}L={anbn∣n≥0} is
decidable because a TM can check equal numbers of a’s and b’s in finite
steps.
• Undecidable Languages:
• A language is undecidable if there is no algorithm (or TM) that can decide
whether a given string belongs to it for all inputs.
• Example:
The Halting Problem (H) = { ⟨M, w⟩ | M halts on input w } is undecidable
because no machine can determine whether another TM will halt on a given
input.

subject: Theory of Computation
text:
Complexity Theory
• Complexity Theory classifies problems based on the resources (time and
space) required to solve them.
• Time Complexity: Measures how the runtime of an algorithm grows with
input size.
• Space Complexity: Measures how much memory an algorithm uses.
• Key Complexity Classes:
• P (Polynomial Time): Problems solvable in polynomial time by a deterministic TM.
Example: Sorting, Matrix Multiplication.
• NP (Nondeterministic Polynomial Time): Problems whose solutions can be verified
in polynomial time.
Example: Boolean Satisfiability Problem (SAT).

subject: Theory of Computation
text:
The Complexity Class NP
• A problem is in NP if there exists a deterministic algorithm that can verify
the correctness of a given solution in polynomial time.
• Formally,
• L∈NP ⟺ ∃ polynomial-time verifier V(x,y)
• such that x∈L
• if and only if there exists a certificate y where V(x,y)=1
• Example:
The Subset Sum Problem: Given a set of integers, determine if there exists
a subset whose sum equals a given number.
• Checking a guessed subset (certificate) can be done in polynomial time.

subject: Theory of Computation
text:
• NP-Completeness and Reducibility
• a) Reducibility
• A problem A is polynomial-time reducible to another problem B
(written as A≤pB) if a polynomial-time algorithm can convert any
instance of A into an instance of B such that solving B also solves A.
• This concept is essential for comparing the difficulty of problems.

subject: Theory of Computation
text:
• b) NP-Complete Problems
• A problem X is NP-Complete if:
• X ∈ N, and
• Every problem Y ∈ NP can be reduced to X in polynomial time.
• In other words, NP-complete problems are the hardest problems in
NP. If one NP-complete problem can be solved in polynomial time,
then P = NP.

subject: Theory of Computation
text:
• Examples of NP-Complete Problems:
• SAT (Boolean Satisfiability Problem) – First proven NP-complete by
Cook-Levin theorem.
• 3-SAT Problem
• Clique Problem
• Vertex Cover Problem
• Subset Sum Problem
• Travelling Salesman Problem (Decision Version)

subject: Theory of Computation
text:
• NP-Hard Problems
• A problem is NP-Hard if every problem in NP can be reduced to it, but
it is not necessarily in NP itself (i.e., its solution might not be
verifiable in polynomial time).
• Example: Optimization version of the Travelling Salesman Problem
(TSP).

First, one needs to show that the problem in question is in NP; i.e., a randomly generated string can be checked in polynomial time to determine whether or not it represents a solution to the problem. Typically, this step is easy. 2. The second step is to show that every problem in NP is reducible to the problem in question in polynomial time. Because of the transitivity of polynomial reduction, this step can be done by showing that a known NP-complete problem can be transformed to the problem in question in polynomial time. The definition of NP-completeness immediately implies that if there exists a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm for just one NP-complete problem, then every problem in NP can be solved in polynomial time

Chomsky Normal Form
• Chomsky Normal Form (CNF) is a simple and
useful form of a CFG
• Every rule of a CNF grammar is in the form
A(cid:198)BC
A(cid:198)a
• Where “a” is any terminal and A,B,C are any
variables except B and C may not be the start
variable
– There are two and only two variables on the right hand
side of the rule
– Exception: S(cid:198)ε is permitted where S is the start variable

Why is this useful?
• Because we know lots of things about binary trees
• We can now apply these things to context-free
grammars since any CFG can be placed into the
CNF format
• For example
– If yield of the tree is a terminal string w
– If n is the height of the longest path in the tree
– Then |w| ≤ 2n-1
– How is this so? (Next slide)

subject: Theory of Computation
text:
Yield of a CNF Parse Tree
• Yield of a CNF parse tree is |w| ≤ 2n-1
• Base Case: n = 1
– If the longest path is of length 1, we must be using the rule A(cid:198)t
so |w| is 1 and 21-1= 1
• Induction
– Longest path has length n, where n>1. The root uses a production
that must be of the form A(cid:198)BC since we can’t have a terminal
from the root
– By induction, the subtrees from B and C have yields of length at
most 2n-2 since we used one of the edges from the root to these
subtrees
– The yield of the entire tree is the concatenation of these two yields,
which is 2n-2 + 2n-2 which equals 2*2n-2 = 2n-2+1=2n-1

subject: Theory of Computation
text:
The Pumping Lemma for CFL’s
• The result from the previous slide (|w| ≤ 2n-1) lets us define
the pumping lemma for CFL’s
• The pumping lemma gives us a technique to show that
certain languages are not context free
– Just like we used the pumping lemma to show certain languages
are not regular
– But the pumping lemma for CFL’s is a bit more complicated than
the pumping lemma for regular languages
• Informally
– The pumping lemma for CFL’s states that for sufficiently long
strings in a CFL, we can find two, short, nearby substrings that we
can “pump” in tandem and the resulting string must also be in the
language.

subject: Theory of Computation
text:
The Pumping Lemma for CFL’s
• Let L be a CFL. Then there exists a constant p
such that if z is any string in L where |z| ≥ p, then
we can write z = uvwxy subject to the following
conditions:
1. |vwx| ≤ p. This says the middle portion is not larger
than p.
2. vx ≠ ε. We’ll pump v and x. One may be empty, but
both may not be empty.
3. For all i ≥ 0, uviwxiy is also in L. That is, we pump
both v and x.

subject: Theory of Computation
text:
Why does the Pumping Lemma
Hold?
• Given any context free grammar G, we can convert it to CNF. The
parse tree creates a binary tree.
• Let G have m variables. Choose this as the value for the longest path
in the tree.
– The constant p can then be selected where p = 2m.
– Suppose a string z = uvwxy where |z| ≥ p is in L(G)
• We showed previously that a string in L of length m or less must have a yield
of 2m-1 or less.
• Since p = 2m, then 2m-1 is equal to p/2.
• This means that z is too long to be yielded from a parse tree of length m.
– What about a parse tree of length m+1?
• Choose longest path to be m+1, yield must then be 2m or less
• Given p=2m and |z| ≤ p this works out
• Any parse tree that yields z must have a path of length at least m+1. This is
illustrated in the following figure:

Pumping Lemma
• We have now shown all conditions of the pumping lemma
for context free languages
• To show a language is not context free we
– Pick a language L to show that it is not a CFL
– Then some p must exist, indicating the maximum yield and length
of the parse tree
– We pick the string z, and may use p as a parameter
– Break z into uvwxy subject to the pumping lemma constraints
• |vwx| ≤ p, |vx| ≠ ε
– We win by picking i and showing that uviwxiy is not in L,
therefore L is not context free

text:
Context Free Languages
• Regular Languages are represented by regular
expressions
• Context Free Languages are represented by a
context-free grammar
• There are context-free languages that are not
regular.
• Finite automata cannot recognize all context-free
languages.
• Context Free Languages are accepted by pushdown
automata, which are non-deterministic finite state
automata with a stack as auxiliary memory.
• Pushdown automata which are deterministic can
represent some but not all of the context-free
languages.
*

text:
Memory
• What kind of memory do we need to be able to
recognize strings in L, using a single left-to-right
pass?
• Example: aaabbcbbaaa
• We need to remember what we saw before the
c
• We could push the first part of the string onto a
stack and, when the c is encountered, start
popping characters off of the stack and
matching them with each character from the
center of the string on to the end.
• If everything matches, this string is an odd
palindrome.
*

subject: Theory of Computation
text:
Counting
• We can use a stack for counting out equal
numbers of a’s and b’s on different sides of a
center marker.
• Example: L = a n cb n aaaacbbbb
• Push the a’s onto the stack until you see a c,
then pop an a off and match it with a b
whenever you see a b.
• If we finish processing the string successfully
(and there are no more a’s on our stack), then
the string belongs to L.
*

text:
Production rules
•Note that in an FSA, each rule told us that
when we were in a given state and saw a
specific character, we moved to a specified
state.
•In a PDA, we also need to know what is on
the stack before we can decide what new
state to move to. After moving to the new
state, we also need to decide what to do
with the stack.
*

subject: Theory of Computation
text:
Working with a stack:
• You can only access the top element of the stack.
• To access the top element of the stack, you have
to POP it off the stack.
• Once the top element of the stack has been
Popped, if you want to save it, you need to PUSH
it back onto the stack immediately.
• Characters from the input string must be read one
character at a time.
• The current configuration of the machine
includes: the current state, the remaining
characters left in the input string, and the entire
contents of the stack

A class of problems with two outputs(yes/no) is said
to be solvable (decidable) if there exists some definite
algorithm which always terminates(halts) with two
outputs (yes/no).
Otherwise, the class of problems is said to be unsolvable
(undecidable).

subject: Theory of Computation
text:
Recursive Enumerable (RE) or Type -0
Language
• In simple words, a "language" is a collection of strings, like words in a
dictionary.
• RE languages or type-0 languages are generated by type-0 grammars. A RE
language can be accepted or recognized by Turing machine which means it
will enter into final state for the strings of language and may or may not
enter into rejecting state for the strings which are not part of the language.
It means TM can loop forever for the strings which are not a part of the
language. RE languages are also called as Turing recognizable languages.
• A recursively enumerable language is a language where we can create a
computer program (or a Turing machine) that can systematically list out all
the strings that belong to the language.

text:
Recursive Enumerable (RE) or Type -0 Language
• A machine that can generate all the possible sentences in the English
language, one by one. This machine wouldn't necessarily know which
sentences are not in the English language, but it could list out all the
valid sentences. This is the idea of a recursively enumerable language.
It can enumerate all the strings that are part of the language.

text:
Closure Properties of Recursive Languages
• Union
• If L1 and L2 are two recursive languages, their union (L1 ∪ L2) is also
recursive. Imagine a machine that checks if a string belongs to L1 or L2; if it
does, it accepts. Since both machines for L1 and L2 will eventually halt, this
combined machine will also halt, making the union recursive.
• Concatenation
• If L1 and L2 are two recursive languages, their concatenation (L1.L2) is also
recursive. Imagine a machine that first checks if the first part of the string
belongs to L1, and if it does, it checks the remaining part of the string for L2.
Since both L1 and L2 machines halt, this combined machine will also halt.

text:
Closure Properties of Recursive Languages
• Kleen Closure
• If L1 is a recursive language, its Kleen closure (L1*) is also recursive. This
means the language including all possible combinations of strings from L1
concatenated together, including the empty string, is also recursive.
• Intersection
• If L1 and L2 are two recursive languages, their intersection (L1 ∩ L2) is also
recursive. Imagine a machine that checks if a string belongs to both L1 and L2.
Since both L1 and L2 machines halt, this combined machine will also halt.
• Complement
• If L1 is a recursive language, its complement (L1') is also recursive. This means
the language containing all strings *not* in L1 is also recursive.

Implementation of UTM
• A UTM Mu then has an input alphabet = {0, 1} and the structure of a
multi-tape TM.
• Mu looks first at the contents of Tape 2 and Tape 3 to determine the
instantaneous description (ID) of M.
• It then consults Tape1 to see what M would do with this ID.
• Finally, Tape 2 and Tape 3 will be modified to reflect the result of the
move.

text:
Summary
• How it works
• A UTM has an infinite tape, a read/write head, and a control unit, just like a
standard Turing machine.
• However, a UTM's input is not just a string of symbols; it's a pair of strings:
• The program: A description of another Turing machine (M). This description
includes (M)'s states, symbols, and transition rules.
• The input: The string (W) that (M) would normally operate on.
• The UTM then simulates the step-by-step execution of machine (M) on input
(W).
• If (M) halts and accepts (W), the UTM will also halt and accept.
• If (M) halts and rejects (W), the UTM will halt and reject.
• If (M) never halts on (W), the UTM will also never halt.

text:
1.1 Reading Files Line by Line
• The standard method for reading a file uses a while loop combined with the read
command and input redirection (<). This approach is crucial because it safely
processes files without issues caused by spaces, tabs, or special characters in
filenames or content.
• Key Techniques:
(cid:0) Input Field Separator (IFS): Setting IFS= prevents leading/trailing whitespace from
being unintentionally stripped from lines.
(cid:0) Raw Read (-r): The -r flag prevents backslash characters from being interpreted as
escape sequences, ensuring the line is read exactly as it appears in the file.

source_path: dataset\study_material\CSE\3\Unix Programming Lab\Lectures\LEC 10 File Handling & Automation.pdf

subject: Unix Programming Lab
text:
1.1 Reading Files Line by Line
• The standard approach uses a while loop to safely process file
content, assigning each line to a variable.
Command syntax : while IFS= read -r line; do ... done < filename
One-Line Illustration :
while IFS= read -r line; do echo "Got: $line"; done < data.txt
Explanation : This robust structure reads data.txt line by line. The echo
command inside the loop executes for every line found in the file.

text:
1.2 Writing to Files (Redirection)
• Output redirection is the core of writing files. Commands (like echo or cat)
generate output, which is then directed away from the standard output (the
terminal) into a file.
(cid:0) Overwriting (>): The single greater-than sign overwrites a file. If the file exists, its
contents are completely deleted before the new data is written. If the file does not
exist, it is created.
(cid:0) Appending (>>): The double greater-than sign appends data. New data is added to
the end of the existing file, preserving the previous content. This is essential for
logging and historical data tracking.
(cid:0) Here Documents (<< EOF): This is a specialized redirection method used to provide
multiple lines of input (often configuration or report text) directly within the script
to a command, typically cat, which then writes the block to a file.

• The find command searches the directory hierarchy for files based on their

directory), size (-size), modification time (-mtime), and permissions (-perm).

text:
3.1 Recurring Jobs with cron
cron is the primary service for scheduling tasks that need to run repeatedly and
reliably (e.g., daily backups, hourly system checks).
(cid:0) Mechanism: Jobs are defined in the crontab (cron table) file. Each entry consists
of six fields defining the schedule, followed by the command to execute.
(cid:0) Crontab Fields: They represent the Minute, Hour, Day of Month, Month, and Day
of Week, followed by the command. Special characters like the asterisk (* for
every value) and the slash (/ for step values, e.g., every 15 minutes) allow for
complex scheduling.
(cid:0) Environment: Cron jobs execute in a minimal shell environment, making it
mandatory to use absolute paths for all commands and scripts to ensure they
execute correctly.

text:
Regular Expressions – grep, sed, awk
• Regular Expressions or regex is a concise way to describe or match text
patterns.
• BRE (Basic Regular Expressions) : classic sed/grep default (POSIX BRE).
Many metacharacters need \ to be special.
• ERE (Extended Regular Expressions) : used by egrep / grep -E / awk (POSIX
ERE). More meta-chars without backslashes.
• PCRE (Perl Compatible Regular Expressions) : most powerful (lookarounds,
non-capturing groups); grep -P (GNU grep) supports PCRE. Not universally
available on all systems.

source_path: dataset\study_material\CSE\3\Unix Programming Lab\Lectures\Lec 11 Shell Scripting advanced topics.pptm.pdf
source_rel_path: CSE\3\Unix Programming Lab\Lectures\Lec 11 Shell Scripting advanced topics.pptm.pdf
subject: Unix Programming Lab
text:
• Core building blocks:
• Literals: foo matches exactly foo.
• Character classes: [abc], ranges [a-z], negation [^0-9].
• Metacharacters:
• . — any single character (except newline in many flavors).
• ^ — start of line/string.
• $ — end of line/string.
• Quantifiers:
• * — 0 or more
• + — 1 or more
• ? — 0 or 1
• {m}, {m,}, {m,n} — exact/repeat/min-max

source_path: dataset\study_material\CSE\3\Unix Programming Lab\Lectures\Lec 11 Shell Scripting advanced topics.pptm.pdf
source_rel_path: CSE\3\Unix Programming Lab\Lectures\Lec 11 Shell Scripting advanced topics.pptm.pdf
subject: Unix Programming Lab
text:
Grep command
• Searches files or stdin for lines that match a regex and prints the matching
lines (by default).
-i: case sensitive -r / -R : recursive search through directories
-v : invert match (show lines that do not match) -l : list filenames that contain a match (once
each)
-E : use ERE (extended) -L : list filenames that do not contain match
-F : fixed strings (fast; no regex, like fgrep) -c : count matching lines per file
-n : show line numbers -o : only print the matched portion (useful for
extracting tokens)
-H : show filename (useful when multiple files) -m N : stop after N matches
-h : suppress filename --color=auto : highlight matches in output
(commonly used; depends on grep build)

source_path: dataset\study_material\CSE\3\Unix Programming Lab\Lectures\Lec 11 Shell Scripting advanced topics.pptm.pdf
source_rel_path: CSE\3\Unix Programming Lab\Lectures\Lec 11 Shell Scripting advanced topics.pptm.pdf
subject: Unix Programming Lab
text:
Examples
• Find lines containing error (case-insensitive) in log files:
grep -i 'error' /var/log/syslog
• Show line numbers:
grep -n 'TODO' *.c
• Search recursively for main:
grep -R --include='*.c' --include='*.h' -n 'main(' .
• List files that contain TODO:
grep -l 'TODO' -R .
• Exit codes (useful in scripts)
• 0 : found match(es)
• 1 : no match
• >1 : error

source_path: dataset\study_material\CSE\3\Unix Programming Lab\Lectures\Lec 11 Shell Scripting advanced topics.pptm.pdf
source_rel_path: CSE\3\Unix Programming Lab\Lectures\Lec 11 Shell Scripting advanced topics.pptm.pdf
subject: Unix Programming Lab
text:
Sed Command
• Reads input line-by-line, applies editing commands (substitute, delete, insert, etc.),
prints result.
• Basic command form
sed 's/regex/replacement/flags' infile
# or with -e for multiple commands
sed -e 's/foo/bar/g' -e '2,5d' file
• Options:
• -n : suppress automatic printing (useful with p commands)
• -e : add script (useful for multiple commands)
• -f scriptfile : read sed commands from file
• -i[SUFFIX] : in-place edit (GNU/BSD differences: BSD sed -i '' to avoid creating
backup)
• -r or -E : use extended regex (GNU -r legacy; POSIX -E is portable)
Note: -E is the POSIX option; prefer sed -E if available.

source_path: dataset\study_material\CSE\3\Unix Programming Lab\Lectures\Lec 11 Shell Scripting advanced topics.pptm.pdf
source_rel_path: CSE\3\Unix Programming Lab\Lectures\Lec 11 Shell Scripting advanced topics.pptm.pdf
subject: Unix Programming Lab
text:
Awk command
• awk is both a language and a tool designed for field-oriented text processing.
It reads input line-by-line, splits each line into fields, and executes
patterns/actions.
• Exceptionally powerful for reports, column transformation, arithmetic, and
structured parsing.
• Classic usage:
awk 'pattern { action }' file
• awk variants:
awk (POSIX), gawk (GNU awk), gawk has many extensions.

source_path: dataset\study_material\CSE\3\Unix Programming Lab\Lectures\Lec 11 Shell Scripting advanced topics.pptm.pdf
source_rel_path: CSE\3\Unix Programming Lab\Lectures\Lec 11 Shell Scripting advanced topics.pptm.pdf
subject: Unix Programming Lab
text:
• Structure
• BEGIN { ... } : run before processing any input (e.g., set FS, print header)
• pattern { action } : for each line that matches pattern run action
• END { ... } : run after processing input (e.g., totals, footers)
• Variables:
$0 — whole line FS — field separator
$1, $2, ... — fields (default FS is whitespace) RS — record separator (default newline)
NF — number of fields OFS — output field separator
NR — number of records (lines) processed ORS — output record separator
Options
• -F FS : set input field separator
• -v var=val : pass shell variables to awk
• -f scriptfile : read awk program from file

source_path: dataset\study_material\CSE\3\Unix Programming Lab\Lectures\Lec 11 Shell Scripting advanced topics.pptm.pdf
source_rel_path: CSE\3\Unix Programming Lab\Lectures\Lec 11 Shell Scripting advanced topics.pptm.pdf
subject: Unix Programming Lab
text:
Examples
• Print 1st field of each line:
awk '{ print $1 }' file
• Print lines where 3rd field > 100:
awk '$3 > 100 { print $0 }' file
• Sum a column (e.g., column 2) and print total:
awk '{ total += $2 } END { print total }' file
• Use custom FS (CSV):
awk -F, '{ print $1, $3 }' file.csv
• Pretty printing with OFS
awk -F: 'BEGIN { OFS="\t" } { print $1, $3, $6 }' /etc/passwd
• Pass shell variable safely:
min=100
awk -v min="$min" '$2 >= min { print $0 }' file

source_path: dataset\study_material\CSE\3\Unix Programming Lab\Lectures\Lec 11 Shell Scripting advanced topics.pptm.pdf
source_rel_path: CSE\3\Unix Programming Lab\Lectures\Lec 11 Shell Scripting advanced topics.pptm.pdf
subject: Unix Programming Lab
text:
Debugging
• Debugging is the process of finding and fixing problems (bugs) in
code. For shell scripts that usually means:
• locating the line(s) that behave unexpectedly,
• inspecting variables and command expansions,
• understanding command exit statuses and control flow,
• reproducing a failure consistently.

source_path: dataset\study_material\CSE\3\Unix Programming Lab\Lectures\Lec 11 Shell Scripting advanced topics.pptm.pdf
source_rel_path: CSE\3\Unix Programming Lab\Lectures\Lec 11 Shell Scripting advanced topics.pptm.pdf
subject: Unix Programming Lab
text:
The central built-in tool: bash -x (and set -x)
• It prints each command after expansions but before execution, prefixed
with a trace marker (by default + ). This shows the actual command being
executed with variables expanded.
• That makes it far easier to see why a command failed (wrong variable,
incorrectly quoted word-splitting, unexpected argument, etc.).
• Example: run a script under xtrace:
bash -x myscript.sh
Bash starts, enables xtrace for the whole run, then reads and executes
myscript.sh.
• NOTE: In the output, The lines beginning with + are the trace lines showing
the command after expansions.

source_path: dataset\study_material\CSE\3\Unix Programming Lab\Lectures\Lec 11 Shell Scripting advanced topics.pptm.pdf
source_rel_path: CSE\3\Unix Programming Lab\Lectures\Lec 11 Shell Scripting advanced topics.pptm.pdf
subject: Unix Programming Lab
text:
• Example B — enable trace inside a script:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set –x # set builtin, -x flag: enable xtrace from this point onward.
a="hello world"
echo "$a“ #prints expanded variable (trace shows echo hello world then output).
set +x #set with +x disables xtrace (turns off the prints).
echo "done“ # runs normally without trace after +x.
Run:
./myscript.sh

source_path: dataset\study_material\CSE\3\Unix Programming Lab\Lectures\Lec 11 Shell Scripting advanced topics.pptm.pdf
source_rel_path: CSE\3\Unix Programming Lab\Lectures\Lec 11 Shell Scripting advanced topics.pptm.pdf
subject: Unix Programming Lab
text:
Example
• Script copyfiles.sh (buggy): • Run under xtrace:
#!/usr/bin/env bash • bash -x copyfiles.sh
FILES="file a.txt file b.txt" • Trace shows:
for f in $FILES; do + FILES='file a.txt file b.txt'
cp "$f" /tmp/ + for f in file a.txt file b.txt
done + cp file /tmp/
• Problem: filenames with spaces + cp a.txt /tmp/
get split incorrectly.
+ cp file /tmp/
+ cp b.txt /tmp/

source_path: dataset\study_material\CSE\3\Unix Programming Lab\Lectures\Lec 11 Shell Scripting advanced topics.pptm.pdf
source_rel_path: CSE\3\Unix Programming Lab\Lectures\Lec 11 Shell Scripting advanced topics.pptm.pdf
subject: Unix Programming Lab
text:
Error Handling
• In shell scripting, error handling means detecting and managing
errors that occur when commands fail.
• Every command in UNIX/Linux returns an exit status code:
• 0 : success
• Non-zero (e.g., 1, 2, 127) : error
• By default, a shell script continues executing even if a command
fails, which can cause unintended behavior.
• So, error handling ensures that when something fails, the script
behaves appropriately, stops, retries, logs an error, or takes an
alternate action.

source_path: dataset\study_material\CSE\3\Unix Programming Lab\Lectures\Lec 11 Shell Scripting advanced topics.pptm.pdf
source_rel_path: CSE\3\Unix Programming Lab\Lectures\Lec 11 Shell Scripting advanced topics.pptm.pdf
subject: Unix Programming Lab
text:
Logical Operators for Error Handling
1. && : Run next command only if previous succeeds
mkdir test_dir && cd test_dir && touch file.txt
• If any step fails (for ex, mkdir couldn’t create folder), the next commands
are skipped.
2. || : Run next command only if previous fails
mkdir /protected_dir || echo "Could not create directory!"
3. Combining && and ||
• Both can be combined to mimic if-else logic:
mkdir test && echo "Directory created" || echo "Failed to create directory"

subject: Unix Programming Lab
text:
What is an array?
An array is a single variable that can hold multiple values (a collection). In Bash, arrays are indexed (numeric indices starting from 0) or
associative (string keys, Bash 4+).
● Indexed arrays: arr=(a b c)
● Associative arrays: declare -A map (Bash 4+)
Note: Arrays are a Bash feature. Portable /bin/sh scripts typically do not support arrays.
Why use arrays?
● Store lists (filenames, user names, numbers) in one variable.
● Easier iteration and batch processing.
● Better structure than many separate scalar variables.

subject: Unix Programming Lab
text:
Creating (declaring) arrays
1. Explicit assignment (preferred shorthand)
# Create an indexed array with four elements
arr=(apple banana cherry "fruit salad")
1. Assign element-by-element
# Put value into index 0
arr[0]=apple
arr[1]=banana
arr[5]=grape
1. Declare an empty array and append later
declare -a list # optional: declare as an indexed array (for clarity)
list=() # empty array
list+=(one) # append 'one'
list+=(two three)
1. Create array from command output
arr=(red green blue)
echo "\${arr[0]}" # prints 'red'
echo ${arr[@]} # word-splits and expands each element
echo "\${arr[@]}" # each element preserved as a single word
echo "\${arr[*]}" # joins elements with first character of IFS (default space)

arr[1]=99

function is executing.

text:
Unix Programming with Standard
Input and Output

subject: Unix Programming Lab
text:
Introduction to Standard Streams
• In Unix systems, communication between
applications is achieved using standard streams:
• • stdin – Standard Input Stream
• • stdout – Standard Output Stream
• • stderr – Standard Error Stream
• These streams act as communication channels
between programs and the terminal.

subject: Unix Programming Lab
text:
Input/Output Streams Example
• Example: Using grep with input redirection
• #!/usr/bin/env bash
• echo pattern | grep pattern
• • 'echo pattern' sends output to grep via
stdin.
• • grep outputs matching results to stdout.

subject: Unix Programming Lab
text: • The script running at the console:

subject: Unix Programming Lab
text:
Error Stream Example
• stderr is used for reporting errors independently
from stdout.
• Example:
• ls > /tmp/log
• ls /not/existed_path > /tmp/log
• • Errors are displayed on console because they
use stderr.

subject: Unix Programming Lab
text:
Redirecting Streams
It is possible to manipulate the standard streams: redirect
them or use pipes to process them.
• Streams can be redirected or piped:
• '>' redirects stdout to a file.
• '2>' redirects stderr.
• '/dev/null' discards unwanted output.
• Example:
• ls /not/existed_path 2> /dev/null

subject: Unix Programming Lab
text:
Discarding Output
In some cases, it is useful to drop all of the
application output (to save storage space or
remove the unimportant sources of data to
analyze). We should remember that we should
mute not just the standard output stream but
the standard error stream also. Let's look at an
example of how does it work.

subject: Unix Programming Lab
text:
• In both lines of script standard output stream redirected to
file /dev/null. This file is not a file itself: but a special Linux
device with a file interface. It has a write function available from
shell (that does nothing). So all of the input is just dropped. But the
second string of the script has a difference from the first one:
"2>&1" at the end of the command. These symbols tell that the
second standard stream ( standard error stream ) needs to be
directed at the first standard stream (standard output stream)
permanently for this command. That is why we see only one error
message displayed in the console - at the second command string
of the script standard error stream redirected to terminating file
device /dev/null in the end.

subject: Unix Programming Lab
text:
Pipelined Streams
• It also can be useful to modify the stream. is
able to run several applications connected by
the streams.

subject: Unix Programming Lab
text:
• The script running at the console:
Here we collect the listing and set “ls” standard output stream as grep
standard input stream by using “|”. On “2>” standard errors stream is
redirected to the termination file. The output stream of grep contains
the "/tmp/a" filename from listing that matches by grep pattern.

subject: Unix Programming Lab
text:
The script running at console.
• As we can see only the second string from 3 of the strings of text for
the grep standard input stream delimited by "EOF" match
the grep pattern: that is why it passed to grep standard output stream and
be displayed in the console next.

subject: Unix Programming Lab
text:
Conclusion
• • Unix uses three main data streams for
process communication.
• • Streams can be redirected, piped, or
discarded as needed.
• • Mastering stdin, stdout, and stderr is
essential for shell scripting.

text:
Linux Commands
UNIX Commands
• A command is a program which interacts with the
kernel to provide the environment and perform the
functions called for by the user.
• A command can be: a built-in shell command; an
executable shell file, known as a shell script; or a
source compiled, object code file.
• The shell is a command line interpreter. The user
interacts with the kernel through the shell. You can
write ASCII (text) scripts to be acted upon by a
shell.

subject: Unix Programming Lab
text:
Linux Commands
UNIX Shell
• The shell sits between you and the operating
system, acting as a command interpreter.
• It reads your terminal input and translates the
commands into actions taken by the system. The
shell is analogous to command.com in DOS.
• When you log into the system you are given a
default shell.
• When the shell starts up it reads its startup files
and may set environment variables, command
search paths, and command aliases, and executes
any commands specified in these files.

subject: Unix Programming Lab
text:
Linux Commands
UNIX Shell
•The original shell was the Bourne shell, sh.
•Every Unix platform will either have the Bourne shell,
or a Bourne compatible shell available.
• The default prompt for the Bourne shell is $ (or #, for
the root user).
• Another popular shell is C Shell. The default prompt
for the C shell is %.

subject: Unix Programming Lab
text:
Linux Commands
UNIX Shell
• Numerous other shells are available from the
network. Almost all of them are based on either
sh or csh with extensions to provide job
control to sh, allow in-line editing of
commands, page through previously executed
commands, provide command name
completion and custom prompt, etc.
• Some of the more well known of these may be
on your favorite Unix system: the Korn shell,
ksh, by David Korn and the Bourne Again
SHell, bash, from the Free Software
Foundations GNU project, both based on sh,
the T-C shell, tcsh, and the extended C shell,
cshe, both based on csh.

subject: Unix Programming Lab
text:
Linux Commands
Shell Programming
• You can write shell programs by creating scripts
containing a series of shell commands.
• The first line of the script should start with #!
which indicates to the kernel that the script is
directly executable.
• You immediately follow this with the name of the
shell, or program (spaces are allowed), to execute,
using the full path name. So to set up a Bourne
shell script the first line would be: #! /bin/sh

subject: Unix Programming Lab
text:
Linux Commands
Shell Programming
• The first line is followed by commands
• Within the scripts # indicates a comment from that
point until the end of the line, with #! being a
special case if found as the first characters of the
file.
#!/bin/bash
cd /tmp
mkdir t
• You also need to specify that the script is
executable by setting the proper bits on the file
with chmod, e.g.:
$ chmod +x shell_script

cd Change the current directory. With no arguments

chmod Change the file permissions.
•
Ex: chmod 751 myfile : change the file permissions to
rwx for owner, rx for group and x for others
Ex: chmod go=+r myfile : Add read permission for the
group and others (character meanings u-user, g-group,
o-other, + add permission,-remove,r-read,w-write,x-exe)
Ex: chmod +s myfile - Setuid bit on the file which allows
the program to run with user or group privileges of the
file.

subject: Unix Programming Lab
text: Linux Commands Linux File Management and Viewing There are three such special permissions within Linux. They are: setuid — used only for applications, this permission indicates that • the application is to run as the owner of the file and not as the user executing the application. It is indicated by the character s in place of the x in the owner category. If the owner of the file does not have execute permissions, the S is capitalized to reflect this fact. setgid — used primarily for applications, this permission indicates • that the application is to run as the group owning the file and not as the group of the user executing the application. The setgid permission is indicated by the character s in place of the x in the group category. If the group owner of the file or directory does not have execute permissions, the S is capitalized to reflect this fact. sticky bit — used primarily on directories, this bit dictates that a file • created in the directory can be removed only by the user that created the file. It is indicated by the character t in place of the x in the everyone category.

text:
Shell scripting
What is a Shell Script or shell scripting
❖ A Shell script can be defined as - "a series of command(s) stored in a plain text file". ❖
Normally shells are interactive. It means the shell will accept command from you (via keyboard)
and execute them. However, if you store a sequence of commands to a text file and tell the shell
to execute the text file instead of entering the commands, that is known as a shell program or
shell script.
❖ Each shell script consists of:
❖ • Shell keywords such as if..else, do..while.
❖ • Shell commands such as pwd, test, echo, continue, type.
❖ • Linux binary commands such as w, who, free etc..
❖ • Text processing utilities such as grep, awk, cut.
❖ • Functions - add frequent actions together via functions. For example, /etc/init.d/functions file
contains functions to be used by most or all system shell scripts in the /etc/init.d directory.
❖ • Control flow statements such as if..then..else or shell loops to preform repeated actions.
Why shell scripting?

subject: Unix Programming Lab
text:
• Shell scripts can take input from a user or file and output them to the screen.
• Whenever you find yourself doing the same task over and over again you should use shell scripting, i.e., repetitive
task automation.
• Creating your own power tools/utilities.
• Automating command input or entry.
• Customizing administrative tasks.
• Creating simple applications.
• Since scripts are well tested, the chances of errors are reduced while configuring services or system
administration tasks such as adding new users.
Advantages: ● Shell scripts can execute without any
additional effort on nearly any modern
● Easy to use.
UNIX / Linux / BSD / Mac OS X
● Quick start, and interactive debugging. ●

interpreted language.
● Sys Admin task automation.

subject: Unix Programming Lab
text:
The #! syntax used in scripts to indicate an interpreter for execution under UNIX / Linux operating
systems. Most Unix shell and perl / python script starts with the following line:
#!/bin/bash OR #!/usr/bin/perl OR #!/usr/bin/python
Starting a Script With #!
1. It is called a shebang or a "bang" line.
2. It is nothing but the absolute path to the Bash interpreter.
3. It consists of a number sign and an exclamation point character (#!), followed by the full path
to the interpreter such as /bin/bash.
4. All scripts under Linux execute using the interpreter specified on a first line.
5. Almost all bash scripts often begin with #!/bin/bash (assuming that Bash has been installed in
/bin)
6. This ensures that Bash will be used to interpret the script, even if it is executed under another
shell.
Shell Comments

subject: Unix Programming Lab
text:
The first line is called a shebang or a "bang" line. The following are the next two
lines of the program:
A word or line beginning with # causes that word and all remaining characters on that line to be ignored. • These lines
aren't statements for the bash to execute. In fact, the bash totally ignores them. • These notes are called comments.
• It is nothing but explanatory text about script.
• It makes source code easier to understand.

Setting up permissions on a script
The chmod command (change mode) is a shell command in Linux. It can change file system modes of files and directories. The modes include
permissions and special modes. Each shell script must have the execute permission. Mode can be either a symbolic representation of changes
to make, or an octal number representing the bit pattern for the new mode bits.

Execute a script
● A shell script can be executed using the following syntax:

subject: Unix Programming Lab
text:
chmod +x script.sh
./script.sh
● You can also run the script directly as follows without setting the script execute permission:
bash script.sh
. script.sh
● In last example, we are using . (dot) command (a.k.a., source) which reads and executes
commands from filename in the current shell. If filename does not contain a slash, directory
names in PATH are used to find the directory containing filename.
● When a script is executed using either the bash command or the dot (.) command. we do
not have to set executable permissions on script.
Debug a script
● You need to run a shell script with -x option from the command line itself:
bash -x script-name OR bash -xv script-name ● You can also modify shebang
line to run an entire script in debugging mode.

How Do I Display The Value Of a Variable?
Use echo command to display variable value. To display the program search path, type:

echo "$PATH"

To display your prompt setting, type:

echo "$Psi"

All variable names must be prefixed with $ symbol, and the entire construct should be enclosed in quotes, Try the
following example to display the value of a variable without using $ prefix:

echo "HOME"
To display the value of a variable with echo $HOME:
echo "$HOME"

You must use $ followed by variable name to print a variable's contents.

The variable name may also be enclosed in braces:

echo "${HOME}"

This is useful when the variable name is followed by a character that could be part of a variable name:

echo "${HOME}work"

Supplies applications with the system calls for file system management.

● Problem: Different File Systems, Different Rules
● Computers can use many types of file systems: ext2, NTFS, FAT32, procfs, etc.
● Each has its own way of storing and retrieving data.
Without a common layer, every program would need to know all of these formats, which is
very messy.
The Virtual File System (VFS) is like a universal translator between programs and all the

Applications use the same commands (open, read, write)

File Type Macros
(<sys/stat.h>)
● In C programming, a macro is like a shortcut name that gets replaced with some
code before the program runs.
● These macros come from the header file <sys/stat.h> and are used to check what type
a file is.
● When we write a C program, we might need to know:
a. Is this file a directory?
b. Is it a normal file?
c. Is it a device?
● The OS stores this information in the file’s metadata.
● We can ask for this metadata with the stat() function, then check the file type with
these macros.

IPC Type Macros
(<sys/stat.h>)
●
IPC = Inter-Process Communication — a way for different programs (processes) to talk to each
other.
● In UNIX, some IPC mechanisms are represented like files — so you can use similar commands to
check or manage them.
Just like we used S_ISREG() to check if something is a regular file, IPC type macros check if a file is
actually:
● A Message Queue → passes messages between processes in order
● A Semaphore → used for locking, to control access to resources
● A Shared Memory Object → memory space that multiple processes can read/write
● Not all UNIX systems treat these IPC objects as files — so these macros may not work
everywhere.
● This is specific to POSIX.1 systems where IPC objects can appear in the filesystem (like in
/dev/mqueue or /dev/shm).

subject: Unix Programming Lab
text:
Superblock
A superblock is a special data structure that holds information about the entire file system.
It’s like the table of contents for the disk — the OS uses it to understand how to read and manage files.
● The OS cannot use the file system if the superblock is missing or corrupted.
ext2/ext4 keep backup copies of the superblock in different places so that if one is damaged, it can be restored.
In memory: struct super_block in the kernel represents a mounted file system.
On disk: Contains permanent info about the file system.
Key fields in struct super_block:
● s_dev → Device identifier
● s_blocksize → Block size in bytes
● s_flags → File system state (read-only, dirty, etc.)
● s_type → File system type (ext2, procfs, etc.)
● s_mounted → Pointer to root inode
● s_op → Pointer to superblock operations (functions for mounting, unmounting, syncing, etc.)

subject: Unix Programming Lab
Unix Programming Lab
text:
Locking/Unlocking superblock
●
In a multitasking OS like UNIX, multiple processes (or threads inside the kernel) might try to read or
modify the same superblock at the same time.
●
If two things change it at once, data can become corrupted.
●
Locking ensures that only one process can access/modify the superblock at a time.
●
WORKING:
The kernel uses a flag inside struct super_block (e.g., s_lock) to mark whether it’s in use.
Locking:
● If s_lock is already set → another process is using it → wait until it’s free.
● If not set → set it to 1 and proceed.
Unlocking:
● Set s_lock back to 0.
● Wake up any processes waiting to use it.

Advantages of inodes
Optimized for file systems with many small files
●
– Each inode can directly point to 48KB of data
– Only one layer of indirection needed for 4MB files
Faster file access
●
– Greater meta-data locality (cid:0) less random seeking
– No need to traverse long, chained FAT entries
Easier free space management
●
– Bitmaps can be cached in memory for fast access
– inode and data space handled independently

text:
PROC FILE SYSTEM
● procfs is a virtual file system — it doesn’t store files on a disk.
● Instead, it’s a way for the kernel to expose information about running processes and system
status as files.
● Usually mounted at /proc.
Structure
● /proc/<PID>/ → Directory for each running process (PID = Process ID).
○ Contains files like:
■ cmdline → Command that started the process
■ status → Process state and memory usage
■ fd/ → File descriptors used by the process
● System-wide info:
○ /proc/cpuinfo → CPU details
○ /proc/meminfo → Memory usage
○ /proc/uptime → How long the system has been running
●

subject: Unix Programming Lab
text:
● Every process has a directory in /proc/pid which contains files relevant
to the process.
How procfs Works Internally
● Mounted during system startup by the kernel.
● In VFS terms:
1. VFS calls read_super() when mounting /proc.
2. proc_read_super() sets up the proc file system’s superblock
in memory.
3. Root inode of /proc is created.
● Files and directories in /proc are generated on the fly when you
open/read them — nothing is stored permanently.

subject: Unix Programming Lab
text:
STRUCTURE OF E2FS
●
ext2 = Second Extended File System, a classic Linux file system.
●
It replaced the older MINIX and ext file systems, which had size and performance limits.
●
Still used today in some cases, and its design influenced ext3 and ext4.
Instead of keeping all inodes in one big table and all data blocks in another far away, ext2 divides the disk into
block groups.
Why?
● Keeps related data close together → reduces disk head movement → faster.
● Balances file placement to avoid fragmentation.
Each block group contains:
1. Superblock copy (for backup)
2. Block group descriptor (info about this group)
3. Block bitmap → Tracks free/used data blocks
4. Inode bitmap → Tracks free/used inodes
5. Inode table → Metadata for files in this group
6. Data blocks → The actual file contents
●

subject: Unix Programming Lab
text:
Directories in ext2
● In ext2, a directory is just a special file.
● Instead of storing text or images, its data blocks contain a list of directory entries.
2. Directory Entry Structure
Each directory entry has:
struct ext2_dir_entry {
unsigned long inode; // Inode number of the file
unsigned short rec_len; // Size of this directory entry
unsigned short name_len; // Length of the file name
char name[EXT2_NAME_LEN]; // The file name itself
};
● inode → Points to the file’s metadata
● rec_len → Lets the OS know where the next entry starts
● name_len → Length of the file name
● name → Actual file name

subject: Unix Programming Lab
text:
Directories in e2fs
What happens on a delete?
ext2 doesn’t shuffle entries around when you delete a file.
Instead:
1. The inode number is set to 0.
2. The previous entry’s rec_len is updated to cover the empty space.
Why?
● Avoids unnecessary moving of data.
● The space can be reused later.

subject: Unix Programming Lab
text:
Block allocation in e2fs
What is Block Allocation?
● When you create or grow a file, the file system must decide which disk blocks to use to store
the file’s data.
● Good allocation = faster file access, less fragmentation.
ext2’s Allocation Goals
● Prevent fragmentation (scattering file pieces all over the disk).
● Keep related data close together for speed.
Target-Oriented Allocation
When ext2 needs a block:
1. First → Look for free space right next to the last block of the file.
2. If not available → Look for a free block within 32 blocks of the last one.
3. If still not found → Use a free block in the same block group.
4. As a last resort → Allocate from another block group.
●

subject: Unix Programming Lab
text:
Pre-allocation (Clustering)
● When ext2 allocates a block, it can reserve up to 8 following blocks if they’re free.
● If the file is closed before all reserved blocks are used → the extra blocks are
released.
● This improves performance for sequential writes.
How ext2 Decides the Target Block
● Let:
○ n = logical block number needed
○ l = last allocated block number
● Target = l + 1 (next block in sequence) if possible.
Visualization
File: report.txt
Allocated: [Block 10][Block 11][Block 12][Block 13]
Instead of: [Block 10] [Block 200] [Block 57] [Block 999]

computer and runs underneath all other programs - without it nothing would
happen at all.

resources on a computer, from the CPU, to memory, to hard disk accesses.

* Tasks the operating system must perform:

different generations and even mutations.

Distribution (BSD) or Linux.

— Others, still contain major portions that are based on the original source code.

In UNIX there are three basic types of files:

Ordinary Files: An ordinary file is a file on the system that contains

data, text, or program instructions. In this tutorial, you look at working
with ordinary files.

Directories: Directories store both special and ordinary files. For users
familiar with Windows or Mac OS, UNIX directories are equivalent to
folders.

Special Files: Some special files provide access to hardware such as hard
drives, CD-ROM drives, modems, and Ethernet adapters. Other special

Starting a Process:
* Foreground Processes:

o By default, every process that you start runs in the foreground. It gets its
input from the keyboard and sends its output to the screen.

* Background Processes:

o A background process runs without being connected to your keyboard. If
the background process requires any keyboard input, it waits.

© The advantage of running a process in the background is that you can run
other commands; you do not have to wait until it completes to start
another!

running in foreground mode.

If a process is running in background mode then first you would need to
get its Job ID using ps command and after that you can use kill command
to kill the process.

text:
What are STDIN, STDOUT, STDERR?
• These are standard data streams in Unix/Linux used for input
and output.
STDIN (Standard Input) – File descriptor 0
STDOUT (Standard Output) – File descriptor 1
STDERR (Standard Error) – File descriptor 2

subject: Unix Programming Lab
text:
STDIN (Standard Input)
Default input source, typically the keyboard.
File descriptor: 0
Used in commands to receive input from user or file.
Example: sort < names.txt

subject: Unix Programming Lab
text:
STDOUT (Standard Output)
Default output destination, typically the terminal.
File descriptor: 1
Used to send results of commands.
Example: ls > files.txt

subject: Unix Programming Lab
text:
STDERR (Standard Error)
Used for outputting error messages.
File descriptor: 2
By default, goes to the terminal like STDOUT.
Example: cat nofile.txt 2> error.txt

subject: Unix Programming Lab
text:
Redirection Examples
1. Redirect STDOUT to a file: command > output.txt
ls > files.txt
This will save the list of files into files.txt instead of displaying it on the screen.
2. Redirect STDERR to a file: command 2> error.txt
cat nofile.txt 2> error.txt
This saves the "No such file or directory" error to error.txt.
3. Redirect both STDOUT and STDERR: command > all.txt 2>&1
ls existing.txt missing.txt > all.txt 2>&1
This command will list existing.txt, and if missing.txt doesn’t exist, the error
will also go into all.txt.
4. Discard errors: command 2>/dev/null
cat file.txt 2>/dev/null
Errors (if any) like "file not found" won't appear on the screen.

text:
What is a Pipe?
• Pipes (`|`) pass output of one command as
input to another.
• Build powerful command chains without temp
files.

subject: Unix Programming Lab
text:
Syntax & How Pipes Work
• command1 | command2
• STDOUT of command1 becomes STDIN for
command2.

subject: Unix Programming Lab
text:
Examples of Pipes
• ls | sort – List and sort files
• cat file.txt | wc -l – Count lines
• ps -ef | grep bash – Filter processes
• ls -l | tee output.txt – Show & save output

subject: Unix Programming Lab
text:
Multiple Pipes
• cat file | sort | uniq | wc -l
• Combines filters for complex tasks.

subject: Unix Programming Lab
text:
Examples
Example 1: Search for a pattern and count lines
cat file.txt | grep "error" | wc -l
Counts how many lines contain the word “error”.
Example 2: Sort and remove duplicate lines
cat names.txt | sort | uniq
Example 3: Display list of logged-in users
who | cut -d' ' -f1 | sort | uniq
Example 4: Count number of words in a file
cat file.txt | wc –w
Example 5: Display IP addresses from ifconfig
ifconfig | grep "inet " | awk '{print $2}'

subject: Unix Programming Lab

Example 3: Stop and resume a background job

jobs

text:
Q5. Based on closest Pair in 1 D.
Since every train takes exactly T hours:
Arrival Time=Departure Time+T
So, minimizing difference in arrival times is equivalent to minimizing:
∣Departure_i − Departure_j|
Thus, the problem reduces to:
Find two departure times with minimum absolute difference.
This is a classic Closest Pair in 1D problem.
Algorithm Idea
1. Sort the departure times
2. Divide the array into two halves
3. Recursively find minimum difference in:
o Left half
o Right half
4. Also check the minimum difference across the boundary
5. Return the minimum of all three
Algorithm Steps [3 marks]
Let D[1…n] be departure times.
Step 1: Sort
Sort D in increasing order
Step 2: Recursive Function
MinDiff(D, low, high):
if high - low <= 1:
return |D[high] - D[low]|
mid = (low + high) / 2
leftMin = MinDiff(D, low, mid)
rightMin = MinDiff(D, mid+1, high)
crossMin = |D[mid+1] - D[mid]|
return min(leftMin, rightMin, crossMin)
