text:
Sed Command
• Reads input line-by-line, applies editing commands (substitute, delete, insert, etc.),
prints result.
• Basic command form
sed 's/regex/replacement/flags' infile
# or with -e for multiple commands
sed -e 's/foo/bar/g' -e '2,5d' file
• Options:
• -n : suppress automatic printing (useful with p commands)
• -e : add script (useful for multiple commands)
• -f scriptfile : read sed commands from file
• -i[SUFFIX] : in-place edit (GNU/BSD differences: BSD sed -i '' to avoid creating
backup)
• -r or -E : use extended regex (GNU -r legacy; POSIX -E is portable)
Note: -E is the POSIX option; prefer sed -E if available.

text:
Awk command
• awk is both a language and a tool designed for field-oriented text processing.
It reads input line-by-line, splits each line into fields, and executes
patterns/actions.
• Exceptionally powerful for reports, column transformation, arithmetic, and
structured parsing.
• Classic usage:
awk 'pattern { action }' file
• awk variants:
awk (POSIX), gawk (GNU awk), gawk has many extensions.

source_path: dataset\study_material\M&C\3\Unix Programming Lab\Lectures\Lec 11 Shell Scripting advanced topics.pptm.pdf
source_rel_path: M&C\3\Unix Programming Lab\Lectures\Lec 11 Shell Scripting advanced topics.pptm.pdf
subject: Unix Programming Lab
text:
• Structure
• BEGIN { ... } : run before processing any input (e.g., set FS, print header)
• pattern { action } : for each line that matches pattern run action
• END { ... } : run after processing input (e.g., totals, footers)
• Variables:
$0 — whole line FS — field separator
$1, $2, ... — fields (default FS is whitespace) RS — record separator (default newline)
NF — number of fields OFS — output field separator
NR — number of records (lines) processed ORS — output record separator
Options
• -F FS : set input field separator
• -v var=val : pass shell variables to awk
• -f scriptfile : read awk program from file

source_path: dataset\study_material\M&C\3\Unix Programming Lab\Lectures\Lec 11 Shell Scripting advanced topics.pptm.pdf

subject: Unix Programming Lab
text:
Examples
• Print 1st field of each line:
awk '{ print $1 }' file
• Print lines where 3rd field > 100:
awk '$3 > 100 { print $0 }' file
• Sum a column (e.g., column 2) and print total:
awk '{ total += $2 } END { print total }' file
• Use custom FS (CSV):
awk -F, '{ print $1, $3 }' file.csv
• Pretty printing with OFS
awk -F: 'BEGIN { OFS="\t" } { print $1, $3, $6 }' /etc/passwd
• Pass shell variable safely:
min=100
awk -v min="$min" '$2 >= min { print $0 }' file

Debugging
• Debugging is the process of finding and fixing problems (bugs) in
code. For shell scripts that usually means:
• locating the line(s) that behave unexpectedly,
• inspecting variables and command expansions,
• understanding command exit statuses and control flow,
• reproducing a failure consistently.

text:
The central built-in tool: bash -x (and set -x)
• It prints each command after expansions but before execution, prefixed
with a trace marker (by default + ). This shows the actual command being
executed with variables expanded.
• That makes it far easier to see why a command failed (wrong variable,
incorrectly quoted word-splitting, unexpected argument, etc.).
• Example: run a script under xtrace:
bash -x myscript.sh
Bash starts, enables xtrace for the whole run, then reads and executes
myscript.sh.
• NOTE: In the output, The lines beginning with + are the trace lines showing
the command after expansions.

source_path: dataset\study_material\M&C\3\Unix Programming Lab\Lectures\Lec 11 Shell Scripting advanced topics.pptm.pdf
source_rel_path: M&C\3\Unix Programming Lab\Lectures\Lec 11 Shell Scripting advanced topics.pptm.pdf
subject: Unix Programming Lab
text:
• Example B — enable trace inside a script:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set –x # set builtin, -x flag: enable xtrace from this point onward.
a="hello world"
echo "$a“ #prints expanded variable (trace shows echo hello world then output).
set +x #set with +x disables xtrace (turns off the prints).
echo "done“ # runs normally without trace after +x.
Run:
./myscript.sh

text:
Error Handling
• In shell scripting, error handling means detecting and managing
errors that occur when commands fail.
• Every command in UNIX/Linux returns an exit status code:
• 0 : success
• Non-zero (e.g., 1, 2, 127) : error
• By default, a shell script continues executing even if a command
fails, which can cause unintended behavior.
• So, error handling ensures that when something fails, the script
behaves appropriately, stops, retries, logs an error, or takes an
alternate action.

source_path: dataset\study_material\M&C\3\Unix Programming Lab\Lectures\Lec 11 Shell Scripting advanced topics.pptm.pdf
source_rel_path: M&C\3\Unix Programming Lab\Lectures\Lec 11 Shell Scripting advanced topics.pptm.pdf

text:
Logical Operators for Error Handling
1. && : Run next command only if previous succeeds
mkdir test_dir && cd test_dir && touch file.txt
• If any step fails (for ex, mkdir couldn’t create folder), the next commands
are skipped.
2. || : Run next command only if previous fails
mkdir /protected_dir || echo "Could not create directory!"
3. Combining && and ||
• Both can be combined to mimic if-else logic:
mkdir test && echo "Directory created" || echo "Failed to create directory"

• set -e : Exit on error-> When you use set -e at the top of your script, it
tells bash:“Exit the script immediately if any command fails.”
#!/bin/bash
set –e # activates strict mode
echo "Start script"
cp file1.txt backup/
echo "File copied"
rm /nonexistent/file # this will fail, script exits immediately
echo "This line will never run“ # never executes

subject: Unix Programming Lab
text:
What is an array?
An array is a single variable that can hold multiple values (a collection). In Bash, arrays are indexed (numeric indices starting from 0) or
associative (string keys, Bash 4+).
● Indexed arrays: arr=(a b c)
● Associative arrays: declare -A map (Bash 4+)
Note: Arrays are a Bash feature. Portable /bin/sh scripts typically do not support arrays.
Why use arrays?
● Store lists (filenames, user names, numbers) in one variable.
● Easier iteration and batch processing.
● Better structure than many separate scalar variables.

subject: Unix Programming Lab
text:
Creating (declaring) arrays
1. Explicit assignment (preferred shorthand)
# Create an indexed array with four elements
arr=(apple banana cherry "fruit salad")
1. Assign element-by-element
# Put value into index 0
arr[0]=apple
arr[1]=banana
arr[5]=grape
1. Declare an empty array and append later
declare -a list # optional: declare as an indexed array (for clarity)
list=() # empty array
list+=(one) # append 'one'
list+=(two three)
1. Create array from command output
arr=(red green blue)
echo "\${arr[0]}" # prints 'red'
echo ${arr[@]} # word-splits and expands each element
echo "\${arr[@]}" # each element preserved as a single word
echo "\${arr[*]}" # joins elements with first character of IFS (default space)

Unix Programming with Standard

subject: Unix Programming Lab
text:
Introduction to Standard Streams
• In Unix systems, communication between
applications is achieved using standard streams:
• • stdin – Standard Input Stream
• • stdout – Standard Output Stream
• • stderr – Standard Error Stream
• These streams act as communication channels
between programs and the terminal.

subject: Unix Programming Lab
text:
Input/Output Streams Example
• Example: Using grep with input redirection
• #!/usr/bin/env bash
• echo pattern | grep pattern
• • 'echo pattern' sends output to grep via
stdin.
• • grep outputs matching results to stdout.

subject: Unix Programming Lab
text: • The script running at the console:

subject: Unix Programming Lab
text:
Error Stream Example
• stderr is used for reporting errors independently
from stdout.
• Example:
• ls > /tmp/log
• ls /not/existed_path > /tmp/log
• • Errors are displayed on console because they
use stderr.

subject: Unix Programming Lab
text:
Redirecting Streams
It is possible to manipulate the standard streams: redirect
them or use pipes to process them.
• Streams can be redirected or piped:
• '>' redirects stdout to a file.
• '2>' redirects stderr.
• '/dev/null' discards unwanted output.
• Example:
• ls /not/existed_path 2> /dev/null

subject: Unix Programming Lab
text:
Discarding Output
In some cases, it is useful to drop all of the
application output (to save storage space or
remove the unimportant sources of data to
analyze). We should remember that we should
mute not just the standard output stream but
the standard error stream also. Let's look at an
example of how does it work.

subject: Unix Programming Lab
text:
• In both lines of script standard output stream redirected to
file /dev/null. This file is not a file itself: but a special Linux
device with a file interface. It has a write function available from
shell (that does nothing). So all of the input is just dropped. But the
second string of the script has a difference from the first one:
"2>&1" at the end of the command. These symbols tell that the
second standard stream ( standard error stream ) needs to be
directed at the first standard stream (standard output stream)
permanently for this command. That is why we see only one error
message displayed in the console - at the second command string
of the script standard error stream redirected to terminating file
device /dev/null in the end.

subject: Unix Programming Lab
text:
Pipelined Streams
• It also can be useful to modify the stream. is
able to run several applications connected by
the streams.

subject: Unix Programming Lab
text:
• The script running at the console:
Here we collect the listing and set “ls” standard output stream as grep
standard input stream by using “|”. On “2>” standard errors stream is
redirected to the termination file. The output stream of grep contains
the "/tmp/a" filename from listing that matches by grep pattern.

subject: Unix Programming Lab
text:
The script running at console.
• As we can see only the second string from 3 of the strings of text for
the grep standard input stream delimited by "EOF" match
the grep pattern: that is why it passed to grep standard output stream and
be displayed in the console next.

subject: Unix Programming Lab
text:
Conclusion
• • Unix uses three main data streams for
process communication.
• • Streams can be redirected, piped, or
discarded as needed.
• • Mastering stdin, stdout, and stderr is
essential for shell scripting.

text:
Linux Commands
UNIX Commands
• A command is a program which interacts with the
kernel to provide the environment and perform the
functions called for by the user.
• A command can be: a built-in shell command; an
executable shell file, known as a shell script; or a
source compiled, object code file.
• The shell is a command line interpreter. The user
interacts with the kernel through the shell. You can
write ASCII (text) scripts to be acted upon by a
shell.

subject: Unix Programming Lab
text:
Linux Commands
UNIX Shell
• The shell sits between you and the operating
system, acting as a command interpreter.
• It reads your terminal input and translates the
commands into actions taken by the system. The
shell is analogous to command.com in DOS.
• When you log into the system you are given a
default shell.

Shell scripting
What is a Shell Script or shell scripting
❖ A Shell script can be defined as - "a series of command(s) stored in a plain text file". ❖
Normally shells are interactive. It means the shell will accept command from you (via keyboard)
and execute them. However, if you store a sequence of commands to a text file and tell the shell
to execute the text file instead of entering the commands, that is known as a shell program or
shell script.
❖ Each shell script consists of:
❖ • Shell keywords such as if..else, do..while.
❖ • Shell commands such as pwd, test, echo, continue, type.
❖ • Linux binary commands such as w, who, free etc..
❖ • Text processing utilities such as grep, awk, cut.
❖ • Functions - add frequent actions together via functions. For example, /etc/init.d/functions file
contains functions to be used by most or all system shell scripts in the /etc/init.d directory.
❖ • Control flow statements such as if..then..else or shell loops to preform repeated actions.
Why shell scripting?

subject: Unix Programming Lab
text:
• Shell scripts can take input from a user or file and output them to the screen.
• Whenever you find yourself doing the same task over and over again you should use shell scripting, i.e., repetitive
task automation.
• Creating your own power tools/utilities.
• Automating command input or entry.
• Customizing administrative tasks.
• Creating simple applications.
• Since scripts are well tested, the chances of errors are reduced while configuring services or system
administration tasks such as adding new users.

additional effort on nearly any modern
● Easy to use.

● Quick start, and interactive debugging. ●

interpreted language.

The #! syntax used in scripts to indicate an interpreter for execution under UNIX / Linux operating

Starting a Script With #!

subject: Unix Programming Lab
text:
Superblock
A superblock is a special data structure that holds information about the entire file system.
It’s like the table of contents for the disk — the OS uses it to understand how to read and manage files.
● The OS cannot use the file system if the superblock is missing or corrupted.
ext2/ext4 keep backup copies of the superblock in different places so that if one is damaged, it can be restored.
In memory: struct super_block in the kernel represents a mounted file system.
On disk: Contains permanent info about the file system.
Key fields in struct super_block:
● s_dev → Device identifier
● s_blocksize → Block size in bytes
● s_flags → File system state (read-only, dirty, etc.)
● s_type → File system type (ext2, procfs, etc.)
● s_mounted → Pointer to root inode
● s_op → Pointer to superblock operations (functions for mounting, unmounting, syncing, etc.)

subject: Unix Programming Lab
Unix Programming Lab
text:
Locking/Unlocking superblock
●
In a multitasking OS like UNIX, multiple processes (or threads inside the kernel) might try to read or
modify the same superblock at the same time.
●
If two things change it at once, data can become corrupted.
●
Locking ensures that only one process can access/modify the superblock at a time.
●
WORKING:
The kernel uses a flag inside struct super_block (e.g., s_lock) to mark whether it’s in use.
Locking:
● If s_lock is already set → another process is using it → wait until it’s free.
● If not set → set it to 1 and proceed.
Unlocking:
● Set s_lock back to 0.
● Wake up any processes waiting to use it.

● procfs is a virtual file system — it doesn’t store files on a disk.
● Instead, it’s a way for the kernel to expose information about running processes and system
status as files.
● Usually mounted at /proc.
Structure
● /proc/<PID>/ → Directory for each running process (PID = Process ID).
○ Contains files like:
■ cmdline → Command that started the process
■ status → Process state and memory usage
■ fd/ → File descriptors used by the process
● System-wide info:
○ /proc/cpuinfo → CPU details
○ /proc/meminfo → Memory usage
○ /proc/uptime → How long the system has been running

subject: Unix Programming Lab
text:
● Every process has a directory in /proc/pid which contains files relevant
to the process.
How procfs Works Internally
● Mounted during system startup by the kernel.
● In VFS terms:
1. VFS calls read_super() when mounting /proc.
2. proc_read_super() sets up the proc file system’s superblock
in memory.
3. Root inode of /proc is created.
● Files and directories in /proc are generated on the fly when you
open/read them — nothing is stored permanently.

subject: Unix Programming Lab
text:
STRUCTURE OF E2FS
●
ext2 = Second Extended File System, a classic Linux file system.
●
It replaced the older MINIX and ext file systems, which had size and performance limits.
●
Still used today in some cases, and its design influenced ext3 and ext4.
Instead of keeping all inodes in one big table and all data blocks in another far away, ext2 divides the disk into
block groups.
Why?
● Keeps related data close together → reduces disk head movement → faster.
● Balances file placement to avoid fragmentation.
Each block group contains:
1. Superblock copy (for backup)
2. Block group descriptor (info about this group)
3. Block bitmap → Tracks free/used data blocks
4. Inode bitmap → Tracks free/used inodes
5. Inode table → Metadata for files in this group
6. Data blocks → The actual file contents
●

subject: Unix Programming Lab
text:
Directories in ext2
● In ext2, a directory is just a special file.
● Instead of storing text or images, its data blocks contain a list of directory entries.
2. Directory Entry Structure
Each directory entry has:
struct ext2_dir_entry {
unsigned long inode; // Inode number of the file
unsigned short rec_len; // Size of this directory entry
unsigned short name_len; // Length of the file name
char name[EXT2_NAME_LEN]; // The file name itself
};
● inode → Points to the file’s metadata
● rec_len → Lets the OS know where the next entry starts
● name_len → Length of the file name
● name → Actual file name

subject: Unix Programming Lab
text:
Directories in e2fs
What happens on a delete?
ext2 doesn’t shuffle entries around when you delete a file.
Instead:
1. The inode number is set to 0.
2. The previous entry’s rec_len is updated to cover the empty space.
Why?
● Avoids unnecessary moving of data.
● The space can be reused later.

subject: Unix Programming Lab
text:
Block allocation in e2fs
What is Block Allocation?
● When you create or grow a file, the file system must decide which disk blocks to use to store
the file’s data.
● Good allocation = faster file access, less fragmentation.
ext2’s Allocation Goals
● Prevent fragmentation (scattering file pieces all over the disk).
● Keep related data close together for speed.
Target-Oriented Allocation
When ext2 needs a block:
1. First → Look for free space right next to the last block of the file.
2. If not available → Look for a free block within 32 blocks of the last one.
3. If still not found → Use a free block in the same block group.
4. As a last resort → Allocate from another block group.
●

subject: Unix Programming Lab
text:
Pre-allocation (Clustering)
● When ext2 allocates a block, it can reserve up to 8 following blocks if they’re free.
● If the file is closed before all reserved blocks are used → the extra blocks are
released.
● This improves performance for sequential writes.
How ext2 Decides the Target Block
● Let:
○ n = logical block number needed
○ l = last allocated block number
● Target = l + 1 (next block in sequence) if possible.
Visualization
File: report.txt
Allocated: [Block 10][Block 11][Block 12][Block 13]
Instead of: [Block 10] [Block 200] [Block 57] [Block 999]

text:
Introduction

* The operating system (OS) is the program which starts up when you turn on your
computer and runs underneath all other programs - without it nothing would
happen at all.

* Insimple terms, an operating system is a manager. It manages all the available
resources on a computer, from the CPU, to memory, to hard disk accesses.

* Tasks the operating system must perform:
— Control Hardware
— Run Applications
— Manage Data and Files
— Security

grown to become the most widely used operating system.

different generations and even mutations.

— Some differ substantially from the original version, like Berkeley Software
Distribution (BSD) or Linux.

— Others, still contain major portions that are based on the original source code.

The swap device is a block device in a configurable section of a disk

Kernel allocates contiguous space on the swap device without
fragmentation

It maintains free space of the swap device in an in-core table, called map
The kernel treats each unit of the swap map as group of disk blocks

As kernel allocates and frees resources, it-updates the map accordingly

text:
What are STDIN, STDOUT, STDERR?
• These are standard data streams in Unix/Linux used for input
and output.
STDIN (Standard Input) – File descriptor 0
STDOUT (Standard Output) – File descriptor 1
STDERR (Standard Error) – File descriptor 2

subject: Unix Programming Lab
text:
STDIN (Standard Input)
Default input source, typically the keyboard.
File descriptor: 0
Used in commands to receive input from user or file.
Example: sort < names.txt

subject: Unix Programming Lab
text:
STDOUT (Standard Output)
Default output destination, typically the terminal.
File descriptor: 1
Used to send results of commands.
Example: ls > files.txt

subject: Unix Programming Lab
text:
STDERR (Standard Error)
Used for outputting error messages.
File descriptor: 2
By default, goes to the terminal like STDOUT.
Example: cat nofile.txt 2> error.txt

subject: Unix Programming Lab
text:
Redirection Examples
1. Redirect STDOUT to a file: command > output.txt
ls > files.txt
This will save the list of files into files.txt instead of displaying it on the screen.
2. Redirect STDERR to a file: command 2> error.txt
cat nofile.txt 2> error.txt
This saves the "No such file or directory" error to error.txt.
3. Redirect both STDOUT and STDERR: command > all.txt 2>&1
ls existing.txt missing.txt > all.txt 2>&1
This command will list existing.txt, and if missing.txt doesn’t exist, the error
will also go into all.txt.
4. Discard errors: command 2>/dev/null
cat file.txt 2>/dev/null
Errors (if any) like "file not found" won't appear on the screen.

subject: Unix Programming Lab
text:

• Pipes (`|`) pass output of one command as
input to another.
• Build powerful command chains without temp
files.

subject: Unix Programming Lab
text:

• command1 | command2
• STDOUT of command1 becomes STDIN for

subject: Unix Programming Lab
text:

subject: Unix Programming Lab
text:

• cat file | sort | uniq | wc -l

subject: Unix Programming Lab
text:
Examples
Example 1: Search for a pattern and count lines
cat file.txt | grep "error" | wc -l
Counts how many lines contain the word “error”.
Example 2: Sort and remove duplicate lines
cat names.txt | sort | uniq
Example 3: Display list of logged-in users
who | cut -d' ' -f1 | sort | uniq
Example 4: Count number of words in a file
cat file.txt | wc –w
Example 5: Display IP addresses from ifconfig
ifconfig | grep "inet " | awk '{print $2}'
